question: What are the symptoms of high blood pressure?
answer: High blood pressure (hypertension) is often called the 'silent killer' because it usually has no symptoms. When symptoms do occur, they may include: severe headaches, nosebleeds, shortness of breath, dizziness, chest pain, visual changes, and blood in urine. Most people discover high blood pressure through routine checkups. That's why regular blood pressure monitoring is essential, especially if you have risk factors like obesity, family history, high salt intake, or sedentary lifestyle.

question: How do I enroll in Medicare?
answer: Medicare enrollment depends on your situation: 1) Automatic enrollment - If you're already receiving Social Security benefits, you'll be automatically enrolled in Medicare Parts A & B when you turn 65. 2) Initial Enrollment Period - 7-month period around your 65th birthday (3 months before, birth month, 3 months after). 3) Special Enrollment Period - If you have employer coverage, you can enroll within 8 months of losing that coverage. 4) General Enrollment Period - January 1 - March 31 annually (coverage starts July 1). Enroll through Social Security (ssa.gov) or your local Social Security office.

question: What is the difference between PPO and HMO plans?
answer: PPO (Preferred Provider Organization): Flexibility to see any doctor without referral, higher premiums and out-of-pocket costs, out-of-network coverage available at higher cost, no primary care physician requirement, good for those who want provider choice. HMO (Health Maintenance Organization): Lower premiums and out-of-pocket costs, must choose a primary care physician (PCP), referrals required for specialists, typically no out-of-network coverage except emergencies, good for those wanting lower costs and coordinated care. Choose based on your healthcare needs, budget, and how important provider flexibility is to you.

question: How should I prepare for surgery?
answer: Surgery preparation checklist: 1) Pre-op appointments - complete all required tests and consultations. 2) Medications - inform your surgeon of all medications; some may need to be stopped (blood thinners, aspirin). 3) Fasting - follow instructions about when to stop eating/drinking (usually midnight before). 4) Arrange help - organize transportation and post-surgery care/help at home. 5) Home preparation - prepare comfortable recovery space, stock up on supplies. 6) Day of surgery - wear comfortable clothes, leave valuables at home, bring insurance cards and ID. 7) Follow pre-op instructions exactly - showering, medications, etc. 8) Ask questions - understand what to expect during and after surgery.

question: What should I look for in a primary care physician?
answer: Choosing a PCP considerations: 1) Network status - ensure they accept your insurance. 2) Location and hours - convenient for regular visits. 3) Board certification - verify credentials and training. 4) Communication style - someone who listens and explains clearly. 5) Hospital affiliations - aligned with quality hospitals if hospitalization needed. 6) Availability - can they see you promptly when sick? 7) Telehealth options - virtual visit availability. 8) Patient reviews - check ratings and feedback. 9) Practice philosophy - preventive care focus, shared decision-making. 10) Languages spoken - if relevant to your needs. Schedule a 'meet and greet' appointment to assess fit before committing.

question: How do I manage asthma effectively?
answer: Asthma management strategies: 1) Know your triggers - allergens, exercise, cold air, smoke, stress - and avoid them when possible. 2) Take medications as prescribed - controller medications daily, rescue inhalers as needed. 3) Use proper inhaler technique - ask your doctor or pharmacist to demonstrate. 4) Have an asthma action plan - written plan for daily management and emergencies. 5) Monitor symptoms - keep a diary, use peak flow meter if recommended. 6) Get vaccinated - flu and pneumonia vaccines reduce infection risk. 7) Maintain healthy weight - obesity can worsen asthma. 8) Manage related conditions - allergies, GERD, sinusitis. 9) Regular check-ups - at least annually to review control and adjust treatment.

question: What are the benefits of breastfeeding?
answer: Breastfeeding benefits for baby: Optimal nutrition tailored to baby's needs, antibodies for immune protection, reduced risk of infections (ear, respiratory, digestive), lower risk of SIDS, allergies, obesity, and diabetes, promotes healthy weight gain, supports brain development. Benefits for mother: Helps uterus contract and reduces bleeding, burns calories (aids weight loss), reduces risk of breast and ovarian cancer, promotes bonding, convenient and cost-effective, may reduce risk of postpartum depression. WHO recommends exclusive breastfeeding for first 6 months, continued with complementary foods up to 2 years or beyond.

question: How do I choose the right health insurance plan?
answer: Health insurance selection tips: 1) Assess your needs - frequency of doctor visits, current medications, planned procedures. 2) Compare plan types - HMO vs PPO vs EPO vs HDHP. 3) Check networks - ensure your doctors and preferred hospitals are in-network. 4) Compare total costs - not just premiums, but also deductibles, copays, coinsurance, and out-of-pocket maximum. 5) Review prescription coverage - check your medications are covered at reasonable cost. 6) Consider HSA eligibility - if you want tax-advantaged savings. 7) Evaluate additional benefits - dental, vision, mental health, telehealth. 8) Review coverage details - what's covered and what's excluded. 9) Read the Summary of Benefits carefully before enrolling.

question: What are the early signs of kidney disease?
answer: Early kidney disease often has no symptoms. When present, signs may include: fatigue and low energy, difficulty concentrating, poor appetite, trouble sleeping, muscle cramps at night, swollen feet and ankles (edema), puffiness around eyes especially in morning, dry and itchy skin, frequent urination especially at night, foamy or bubbly urine (protein in urine), blood in urine. Risk factors include: diabetes, high blood pressure, heart disease, family history, obesity, age 60+. Regular screening (blood and urine tests) is crucial for early detection, especially if you have risk factors.

question: How can I quit smoking successfully?
answer: Smoking cessation strategies: 1) Set a quit date - pick a day within the next 2 weeks. 2) Tell family and friends - build your support network. 3) Anticipate challenges - plan for triggers and cravings. 4) Remove tobacco products - from home, car, and work. 5) Talk to your doctor about: Nicotine replacement therapy (patches, gum, lozenges), prescription medications (Chantix, Wellbutrin), combination approaches. 6) Consider counseling - individual or group support. 7) Use quitlines - 1-800-QUIT-NOW provides free coaching. 8) Try apps - Smoke Free, QuitGuide provide tracking and tips. 9) Handle cravings - they pass in 5-10 minutes; distract yourself, drink water, take deep breaths. 10) Don't give up - most people try several times before succeeding; each attempt teaches you something.
